name: Storyboarding and Pre-visualization
title: Storyboarding and Pre-visualization
answer: Storyboarding and pre-visualization is the practice of turning a script or concept into a sequence of images, panels, animatics, and spatial plans before principal photography or final rendering. It covers shot composition, camera movement, lighting intent, blocking, continuity, and timing, and it sits between writing and production. In AI-assisted cinematography, the same practice extends to generating reference frames, style tests, and rough motion studies that a director and crew can review. The output is not the final film but a shared visual argument that reduces ambiguity for everyone on set or in the pipeline.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of conventional tools and generative systems. Storyboard artists use drawing tablets, 2D and 3D previsualization software, and editing or animatic tools, while AI-assisted workflows add image and video models for frame generation, style transfer, and motion tests. The site currently tracks 1000 live image generation models and 1000 video models, which reflects how quickly the reference-frame and animatic layer has become model-driven. Compute may be local on a workstation or remote through a hosted service, and the choice affects latency, privacy, and how many iterations a team can afford.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pass starts with a script breakdown, shot list, and rough thumbnails, then moves to cleaned panels, camera diagrams, and an animatic timed to dialogue or temp music. When generative models are used, the artist writes prompts or conditions on sketches, depth maps, or existing frames, then curates and edits the results rather than accepting the first output. Consistency is managed with character sheets, style references, seeds, and control images, and the board is revised against editorial feedback. The final previsualization package often includes aspect ratios, lens choices, and notes on transitions so that the shoot or render can follow it.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and provenance matter because storyboards and previsualization frames can incorporate references, likenesses, locations, and styles that belong to someone else. Teams typically keep a record of source material, model versions, prompts, and edits so that a frame can be traced if a question arises. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, which shows that ownership and fair use around generated images and video are still being tested. Clearance for music, trademarks, and performer likeness is handled separately from the visual board, and studio or client policies often determine what can be generated and what must be drawn by hand. In practice, teams document sources and review early, rather than assuming any output is free of claims.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Previsualization is moving toward faster iteration between text, sketch, and motion, with models that can hold a character or camera move across a sequence rather than a single frame. Tighter links are likely between storyboard tools and virtual production, where a board can become a real-time scene or a camera plan for an LED volume. The volume of available image and video models will keep growing, so curation, versioning, and provenance will matter as much as generation. The craft question remains the same, which is whether the board communicates the intended story clearly enough for the people who have to build it.
